opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't uniform. It varied a lot by team, and I think that's natural when you bring together two organizations that each had their own culture, tooling, and way of doing research.

The teams that adjusted fastest were the ones already working toward the same goal, especially the people on large language models. Once leadership made clear that the priority was building one flagship model family together, those groups had a shared target. Combining compute, data pipelines, and evaluation work happened fairly quickly, because everyone could see that duplicating effort on two parallel large models didn't make sense.

Other areas took longer. Brain and DeepMind had different infrastructure histories. There were different codebases, different ways of running experiments, and different conventions for publishing and reviewing work. Merging those isn't something you do with a memo. It takes months of people working out which systems to keep, which to retire, and how to migrate without slowing research down. The more exploratory research groups also needed time to understand where they fit in an organization that had become much more focused on a few big priorities.

Culture was probably the slowest part. Brain had a fairly bottom-up tradition, where researchers had a lot of freedom to pursue their own ideas. DeepMind historically had a more top-down, mission-driven structure. Blending those means negotiating how much autonomy individuals keep and how decisions get made. You can't really rush that. It settles over time through actually shipping things together and building trust.

So overall, the pace was fast where there was urgency and a clear common target, and slower where the questions were about identity, process, and long-term research direction. In hindsight, I think that sequencing made sense: get the most critical joint work moving first, and let the rest catch up.

r001.rationale: The response says teams had to decide which systems to keep or retire and how to migrate, but does not state that they adopted infrastructure that largely displaced what teams had previously built.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that it was really uneven, and I don't think that's a criticism so much as a description of how big organizations actually merge. On paper it happened in 2023 when Google Brain and DeepMind became Google DeepMind, but in practice it was a process that played out over a year or two, and different parts of the organization moved at very different speeds.

The research teams working directly on Gemini, the big frontier model effort, were probably the fastest to adjust, because they had a shared goal that was very concrete and very urgent. When you're racing to train a model and there's a release date, questions about whose codebase or whose culture wins get resolved pretty quickly out of necessity. People just had to sit down together and ship.

The infrastructure side was more complicated. Brain had grown up very deep inside Google's internal stack, TPUs, the whole ecosystem, and DeepMind had its own tooling and ways of working, partly because it had been in London and operating somewhat independently for years. Consolidating that was slower, and I think there were months where people were maintaining two of everything.

And then the parts that moved slowest were the more exploratory research groups and the operational, people-side things. Compensation structures, performance review norms, how you decide what gets published, what the publication culture should even be when you're now competing commercially. Those are culturally loaded, and both sides had strong, legitimate traditions. Brain was very much an open, publish-first culture historically, and DeepMind had more of a long-horizon, mission-driven, somewhat more guarded approach. Reconciling that isn't something you do with an org chart.

So if I had to summarize, the product-facing and model-training work converged fast because the market forced it, and the cultural and research-process integration lagged behind, which I think is fairly normal. The interesting question is whether the slower parts ever fully converge or whether you end up with a kind of hybrid culture that's neither of the originals.

r001.rationale: The candidate says infrastructure consolidation was slow and that teams maintained two of everything for a time. It does not state that integration required adopting infrastructure that would largely displace what teams had previously built.

astra-6.text:
I think the pace varies quite a bit across teams. Bringing two research organizations together isn’t just a matter of changing the reporting structure. People have different ways of running experiments, sharing results, and deciding what to prioritize, and those habits take time to align.

For teams working toward a shared goal, there’s a natural reason to collaborate, so that adjustment can happen relatively quickly. Other teams need more time to understand how their work fits together. I wouldn’t necessarily interpret that difference as a problem. The important thing is to make collaboration easier while preserving the space people need to do good research.

r001.rationale: The response discusses differing team practices and collaboration, but does not state that infrastructure integration required adopting infrastructure that would largely displace what teams had built.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the pace varies quite a bit across teams. For researchers working on similar problems, there’s a fairly natural reason to come together: you can share ideas, learn from each other, and work toward a common goal. But aligning infrastructure, processes, and priorities takes longer, especially when teams have developed different ways of working.

So I wouldn’t describe the integration as something that happens at one uniform speed. Some collaborations can start quickly, while other changes need more time. The important thing is giving people clarity about what they’re trying to accomplish together.
